messages.content:
You are a clinical validator checking whether a PTSD case
vignette accurately reflects a patient's required cognitive connections.

You will receive:
- A vignette to validate
- A list of REQUIRED edges that must appear
- A list of ACTIVE components that must appear

---

COMPONENT SYNONYMS
Each component may appear by its exact name or any accepted synonym:
  Triggers            → "triggers", "reminders", "cues", "triggering stimuli"
  Negative Appraisals → "negative appraisals", "negative beliefs", "appraisals", "distorted beliefs"
  Memory              → "intrusive memory", "trauma memory", "traumatic memory", "the memory"
  Threat              → "sense of threat", "perceived threat", "threat", "feeling of danger"
  Maladaptive Strategies → "maladaptive strategies", "avoidance", "maladaptive coping", "safety behaviours"

---

CAUSAL STANDARD
A required edge A→B is SATISFIED if, within the same paragraph:
  - Both A and B (or their synonyms) appear, AND
  - The paragraph conveys — through any language — that A influences, drives, or leads to B.
This includes direct causal sentences, sequential structure, or connecting phrases
like "because of", "this meant", "so", "which led", "as a result", "consequently", "in turn".
A required edge is MISSING only if no paragraph conveys the A→B relationship at all.

---

SECTION 1 — COMPONENT CHECK
Active components (must appear in the vignette):
  - Maladaptive Strategies
  - Memory
  - Negative Appraisals
  - Triggers

Confirm each component appears as a described feature of the patient's presentation.
This is an internal check only — do NOT add component results to violations.

---

SECTION 2 — REQUIRED EDGES
  - Triggers → Maladaptive Strategies
  - Triggers → Memory
  - Negative Appraisals → Memory
  - Memory → Maladaptive Strategies
  - Memory → Triggers
  - Maladaptive Strategies → Memory
  - Maladaptive Strategies → Negative Appraisals
  - Maladaptive Strategies → Triggers

For each edge, apply the causal standard above.
- If satisfied: do nothing — only failures are reported.
- If missing: add it to violations and explain in one sentence what causal relationship is absent.

Validate the following vignette against the cognitive graph.

Tane, a 74‑year‑old editor from New Zealand’s Northland, first recalls the night when his then‑wife, Mara, turned a quiet evening into a nightmare. She had slipped on a wet floor, slipped, and the fall turned violent; she grabbed him by the arm, yanked his shirt, and slammed his head into a lamp. She hissed, “You always mess things up,” then punched him, leaving a bruise on his cheek and a sense of utter powerlessness. The memory is still a series of still images, each one vivid and disconnected from his own sense of self. When Tane later faces a sharp editorial comment from a colleague, the echo of Mara’s words—“You always mess things up”—rushes in, and he automatically pulls his phone into the kitchen and flips through a crossword, a form of distraction. In the same breath, he avoids looking at any pictures of Mara that still hang in the hallway, and he steers clear of any strong emotional reactions that might surface. The criticism at work, the violence he once endured, and the sight of Mara’s face together trigger these avoidance behaviors, keeping the trauma at bay only by numbing himself. The criticism also pulls Tane back into the event. Each time a reviewer points out a flaw in his copy, he sees the scene of Mara’s hand on his shoulder, the sting of the lamp, the sharp hiss. The vivid snapshot of the night lingers, and the alien quality of the memory makes it feel as though someone else is living the violence in his mind. The trigger of a critique has the same effect as the trigger of violence or seeing the offender’s cue, launching him into the flashback. Tane’s negative appraisals—feeling that he is an object rather than a person, that he will never feel normal emotions again, and that the abuse happened because of who he is—only deepen the memory’s grip. He interprets the flashback as proof of his own failure, a confirmation that he is unworthy and incapable. These appraisals reinforce the sense that the memory does not belong to him, that it is an external condemnation, and this belief pulls the images into his conscious awareness each time he recalls them. When the flashback surfaces, Tane automatically engages in the same distraction and avoidance. The rage he feels at the thought of the lamp striking his head is cut short by turning the TV on or scrolling through old news stories. He keeps his feelings at bay, refusing to let himself feel the anger that the memory conjures. Thus, the memory of the night, with its snapshot quality and alien feel, directly fuels the avoidance behaviors that have become his default coping strategy. The memory’s resurfacing also heightens Tane’s sensitivity to triggers. After a brief recollection of the abuse, a single critical comment at the office feels like a threat of violence, as if the lamp might fall again. The more often the memory appears, the more Tane starts to see criticism itself as a prelude to physical harm, and the triggers and the memory reinforce one another in a tightening loop. Each time Tane distracts himself, avoids any cue of Mara, or denies his feelings, the underlying memory and the negative appraisals become more entrenched. The avoidance shields him from the pain but also keeps the traumatic images fresh, and the sense that he is unworthy and that he has no control over his emotions strengthens. These avoidance tactics, in turn, feed the memory’s vividness, deepen his negative judgments, and make criticism, violence, and offender cues feel even more threatening, closing the vicious circle that has defined his life for decades. Now, weeks after a particularly harsh deadline, Tane is unable to concentrate on a manuscript and has begun skipping meetings. The fear that his rage might erupt at any moment, coupled with the shame that he feels unfit to hold his editorial job, has driven him to seek help. He hopes to regain the calm he once had, to feel his own emotions without the terror of an imagined blow, and to break the cycle that keeps him trapped in a life where a single word of critique can summon a remembered assault.
